content.title: Vector-Valued Motion in AP Calculus BC
content.overview: Vector-valued motion describes the path of a particle in two or three dimensions using a position vector r(t). By applying differentiation componentwise, we can determine the particle's velocity, speed, and acceleration at any given time t.
learning_objectives: Differentiate a position vector r(t) componentwise to find the velocity vector v(t).
Calculate the speed of a particle as the magnitude of the velocity vector at a specific time.
Differentiate the velocity vector componentwise to find the acceleration vector a(t).
Apply correct units for velocity, speed, and acceleration based on the units of position and time.

sections.title: The Hierarchy of Motion Vectors
sections.content:
In vector-valued motion, position is represented by r(t) = ⟨x(t), y(t), z(t)⟩. To find the velocity vector v(t), we differentiate each component with respect to time: v(t) = r'(t) = ⟨x'(t), y'(t), z'(t)⟩. To find the acceleration vector a(t), we differentiate the velocity vector: a(t) = v'(t) = r''(t) = ⟨x''(t), y''(t), z''(t)⟩. Each derivative represents the instantaneous rate of change of the preceding quantity.

![A flow chart showing the relationship between position, velocity, and acceleration vectors.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/384a7555-d747-48e3-b8ca-8f645e69567c-1786519399999-751.webp)

sections.title: Calculating Speed
sections.content: Speed is a scalar quantity representing the magnitude of the velocity vector. Unlike velocity, which has direction, speed is always non-negative. For a velocity vector v(t) = ⟨v_x, v_y, v_z⟩, the speed is calculated using the magnitude formula: |v(t)| = sqrt((v_x)^2 + (v_y)^2 + (v_z)^2). In AP Calculus BC, speed is often requested at a specific time t = c.

sections.title: Units and Dimensional Analysis
sections.content: Consistency in units is vital for motion problems. If position r(t) is measured in meters (m) and time t in seconds (s), then: 1. Velocity components and speed are measured in m/s. 2. Acceleration components are measured in m/s^2. Always verify that the units of speed match the units of the magnitude of velocity.

worked_examples.question: A particle moves with position vector r(t) = ⟨3t^2 - 2t, 4 sin(t), ln(t+2)⟩ meters for t ≥ 0 seconds. Find the speed and the acceleration vector a(t) at t = 1 second. (Use cos(1) ≈ 0.5403 and sin(1) ≈ 0.8415).
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Find the velocity vector v(t) by differentiating r(t) componentwise. v(t) = ⟨d/dt(3t^2 - 2t), d/dt(4 sin t), d/dt(ln(t+2))⟩ = ⟨6t - 2, 4 cos t, 1/(t+2)⟩. Step 2: Evaluate v(t) at t = 1. v(1) = ⟨6(1)-2, 4 cos(1), 1/(1+2)⟩ = ⟨4, 4 cos(1), 1/3⟩. Step 3: Calculate speed |v(1)|. Speed = sqrt(4^2 + (4 cos 1)^2 + (1/3)^2) = sqrt(16 + 16(0.5403)^2 + 0.1111) ≈ sqrt(16 + 4.6708 + 0.1111) ≈ sqrt(20.7819) ≈ 4.560 m/s. Step 4: Find the acceleration vector a(t) by differentiating v(t). a(t) = ⟨d/dt(6t - 2), d/dt(4 cos t), d/dt(1/(t+2))⟩ = ⟨6, -4 sin t, -1/(t+2)^2⟩. Step 5: Evaluate a(t) at t = 1. a(1) = ⟨6, -4 sin(1), -1/(1+2)^2⟩ = ⟨6, -4 sin(1), -1/9⟩ m/s^2.

common_mistakes: Confusing speed with velocity: Velocity is a vector ⟨x', y'⟩, while speed is a scalar magnitude.
Sign errors in differentiation: Forgetting that the derivative of cos(t) is -sin(t).
Incorrect Power Rule application: Differentiating 1/(t+2) as ln(t+2) instead of using the chain rule/power rule to get -1/(t+2)^2 for acceleration.
Omitting units: Providing a numerical value for speed or acceleration without the required distance/time or distance/time^2 labels.
exam_tips: When asked for speed, always look for the magnitude of the velocity vector.
Ensure your calculator is in Radian mode for all trigonometric derivatives in AP Calculus.
If a problem asks for the 'velocity' at a time, provide the vector; if it asks for 'speed', provide the scalar magnitude.
Double-check the components of the acceleration vector for correct signs, especially when involving transcendental functions.
content.recap: To analyze vector-valued motion, differentiate the position vector r(t) once to find the velocity vector v(t) and twice to find the acceleration vector a(t). Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, calculated as the square root of the sum of the squares of the velocity components.

knowledge_claims.content: The velocity vector v(t) is found by differentiating each component of the position vector r(t) with respect to time.
The acceleration vector a(t) is found by differentiating each component of the velocity vector v(t) with respect to time.
Speed is defined as the magnitude of the velocity vector v(t).
For a 2D velocity vector ⟨x'(t), y'(t)⟩, speed is calculated as sqrt([x'(t)]^2 + [y'(t)]^2).
Speed is a scalar quantity and is always non-negative, regardless of the direction of the velocity vector.
If position is in meters and time is in seconds, the units for velocity and speed are meters per second (m/s).
If position is in meters and time is in seconds, the units for acceleration are meters per second squared (m/s^2).
A common error is failing to apply the chain rule when differentiating components like ln(t+2) or sin(kt).

To verify an acceleration vector, ensure that the derivative of the velocity's sine component results in a cosine component, and the derivative of a cosine component results in a negative sine component.
Velocity is a vector indicating both rate and direction of motion, whereas speed indicates only the rate of motion.
To find the acceleration at t = c, one must first find the general acceleration vector a(t) and then substitute c for t.
The notation |v(t)| or ||v(t)|| is used to represent the speed of a particle in vector-valued motion.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Vector-Valued Motion — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Vector-Valued Motion: Differentiating a position vector gives velocity, speed is the magnitude of velocity, and acceleration is the velocity derivative.
options.B: Comparison and Limit Comparison Tests: Positive-term series can inherit convergence or divergence from a benchmark through inequalities or a finite positive ratio limit.
options.C: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuity at a point requires an existing limit equal to the function value, and the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees attained values under interval continuity.
options.D: Implicit Differentiation: When variables are related implicitly, differentiating both sides with respect to the independent variable introduces derivative factors for dependent-variable terms.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Differentiating a position vector gives velocity, speed is the magnitude of velocity, and acceleration is the velocity derivative. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Vector-Valued Motion — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Alternating Series and Error: An alternating series converges when magnitudes decrease to zero, and its truncation error is bounded by the first omitted magnitude.
options.B: Vector-Valued Motion: Differentiating a position vector gives velocity, speed is the magnitude of velocity, and acceleration is the velocity derivative.
options.C: Infinite Limits and Asymptotes: Unbounded function behavior near an input can identify a vertical asymptote, while end behavior can identify horizontal or slant tendencies.
options.D: Derivatives of Inverse Functions: The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero.
